title: System and method for three dimensional model printing

report.headline: Verdict: 'Dead patent with a future' (91/100, high confidence): this core PolyJet-style printing patent ran its full term in a field that still looks very active, but newer patents around it may still be in force.
report.what_it_is: A way to 3D print objects by jetting tiny drops of liquid plastic (photopolymer), smoothing each layer with a roller that can sense when it touches the material, then hardening the layer with light and repeating. It is the kind of process behind Stratasys' PolyJet printers, which jet two or more materials layer by layer.

why_it_died.text: It did not die early. It reached the end of its full 20-year term on 2020-01-18 after the owner, a large company, paid every maintenance fee. That points to a patent the owner valued to the end, not one dropped for lack of money or merit. This is why 'Died for money, not merit' scored only 7.5/15: it simply expired on schedule.

case_for.point: The field looks alive. Later filings kept citing this patent, including filings by unrelated owners after it expired. That gives it full marks for 'Field still alive' and 'Recent momentum'.
Big players appear to still build in this space. General Electric has filed 13 times on top of it since 2019, and Stratasys still sells PolyJet printers that researchers use today.
Current machines appear to still use a roller-leveling step, so the core idea seems to remain relevant rather than obsolete.
The claims were fairly broad at grant and examiners often cited it, which suggests it covered a basic step others build on.

case_against.point: You would compete directly with Stratasys, which owns this line, sells the product and has kept patenting on top of it.
Market size rests on one analyst forecast. Citation counts show technical interest, not proof that buyers will pay for a new entrant.
The patent shows the idea, not the know-how. Reliable jetting, leveling and curing will likely need a lot of your own engineering.

blockers.point: Stratasys filed 85 later patents citing this one that may still be in force. Improvements you would need could be covered.
22 later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force.
The printing method may be open while specific photopolymer materials, formulas or process settings may still be patented. A printer is useless without materials.
Manufacturing know-how is not in the patent. Expect to rebuild process details yourself.

assumption_to_test.assumption: There is a group of buyers, such as labs, design studios or dental and medical model makers, who want multi-material photopolymer jetting at a clearly lower cost than Stratasys and will switch to a new supplier to get it, using materials you can source.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: The tech appears mature and the incumbent already sells it, with many later patents around it. A business only works if a lower price or a specific niche pulls buyers away from an established brand, and if usable materials are available.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks: interview 10-15 current or would-be PolyJet users (university labs, prototyping shops, dental labs) about what they pay, what frustrates them and what price would make them switch. Run a $200 landing page offering 'multi-material jetted prints at X% lower cost' and count sign-ups. Ask two or three photopolymer resin suppliers for quotes and whether their jettable resins have usage limits.

attorney_questions: Which of Stratasys' 85 later citing patents, and the 22 cited third-party patents, appear to still be in force and may cover roller leveling, multi-material jetting or curing steps we would use?
Are there active patents on the photopolymer materials or support materials we would need, and can we buy compatible materials without licensing problems?
In the 3 jurisdictions where this family was filed, has every family member expired, and are there any related continuations still active?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: Sustained technical interest: the patent remains heavily cited, including well after it reached end of term, which suggests the dispense-level-cure layering approach is still a reference point for new work.
General Electric Company is the most visible recent filer building on this patent, which points to industrial or manufacturing interest rather than only hobbyist activity.

The described process appears to be commercially embodied today. Stratasys markets PolyJet printers, which are used in research and include a roller-leveling step similar to the claimed leveling step. The evidence does not establish that these products practice the claims.
The owner valued the patent through its full term. It paid every maintenance fee, claimed large-entity status, and filed the family in 3 jurisdictions.

read.who_is_active: General Electric Company is the leading recent filer citing this patent (13 filings since 2019), and Stratasys actively markets PolyJet material-jetting printers in the field.
read.market_read: Citation momentum after expiry, an established commercial product line in material jetting, and a high revival score all suggest the field is alive rather than abandoned. One third-party forecast puts material jetting at about USD 2.03B in 2025 growing to USD 4.90B by 2030, but that is a single analyst estimate and citations indicate technical interest, not revenue.

web.finding: Stratasys currently markets PolyJet printers, which it describes as a technology for full-color 3D printing and additive manufacturing.
A ScienceDirect paper used a Stratasys J720 PolyJet printer to fabricate all of its test specimens.
Stratasys reseller GoEngineer publishes a tutorial on removing the PolyJet roller bath, which points to a roller-leveling step in current machines.
Mordor Intelligence expects the material jetting 3D printing market to reach USD 2.03 billion in 2025 and USD 4.90 billion by 2030 (19.29% CAGR).
